subsystems.name: Infrared optics
subsystems.role: focuses long-wave infrared radiation (8–14 µm) onto the detector.

subsystems.name: Detector array
subsystems.role: converts infrared radiation into electrical signals using an uncooled microbolometer.
parts: vanadium oxide or amorphous silicon pixels

subsystems.name: Signal processing and electronics
subsystems.role: reads out each pixel, applies calibration, and builds a thermal image.

subsystems.name: Shutter and calibration
subsystems.role: provides a uniform temperature reference for offset correction.

subsystems.name: Display and user interface
subsystems.role: shows the thermal image and allows control of settings.

subsystems.name: Power and housing
subsystems.role: powers the camera and protects it in the field.

buildSteps.title: Design the optical system
buildSteps.detail: Choose a lens material that transmits long-wave infrared (germanium, zinc selenide, or chalcogenide glass). Compute lens shapes and spacing to focus 8–14 µm radiation onto the detector.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the lens
buildSteps.detail: For germanium, use single-point diamond turning; for chalcogenide glass, use precision moulding. Apply anti-reflective coatings to reduce reflection losses at each surface.

buildSteps.title: Make the microbolometer wafer
buildSteps.detail: Deposit a thin film of vanadium oxide or amorphous silicon on a silicon wafer. Use micromachining to create suspended pixels (microbridges) that absorb infrared and heat up. Pixel pitch is typically 12–17 µm.

buildSteps.title: Package the detector
buildSteps.detail: Bond the detector wafer to a readout integrated circuit that measures each pixel's resistance. Seal it in a vacuum package to reduce heat loss. Add a thermoelectric stabiliser to hold a constant operating temperature.

buildSteps.title: Assemble electronics
buildSteps.detail: Connect the detector to a processing board with a microcontroller or FPGA. Add memory, display, buttons, and battery. Write firmware to read the ROIC, apply calibration, and render images.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the camera
buildSteps.detail: Place the camera in front of blackbody sources at known temperatures (for example 20 °C and 50 °C). Record each pixel's response and compute calibration coefficients. Program non-uniformity correction.

buildSteps.title: Final assembly and test
buildSteps.detail: Mount the lens, align it to the detector, install the shutter mechanism, and seal the housing. Test focus, temperature accuracy, and image quality.

prerequisites.why: uncooled thermal detectors work at room temperature, making handheld cameras possible.
germanium and chalcogenide glasses transmit long-wave infrared and can be shaped into lenses.
pixels must be thermally isolated from their surroundings to sense small temperature changes.
handheld devices need processing, display, and battery life in a small package.
accurate temperature measurement requires reference sources at known temperatures.

pathway.milestone: handheld cameras with resolutions from about 160×120 to 640×480 pixels
pathway.unlocks: routine building and electrical inspection for leaks and hot spots.

pathway.milestone: smaller pixels and higher-resolution detectors at lower cost
pathway.unlocks: wider use in maintenance, firefighting, and medical screening.

pathway.milestone: integration into smartphones and drones with on-device AI
pathway.unlocks: automatic fault detection and aerial thermal surveys without extra hardware.

pathway.milestone: multispectral fusion with visible-light cameras and 3D thermal mapping
pathway.unlocks: automated building audits and real-time structural analysis.
